He reports that the problem is causing significant stress in his marriage.
On further questioning, he mentions that he still experiences nocturnal erections and occasionally wakes up with an erection in the morning.
His past medical history is significant for well-controlled hypertension.
He takes for which he takes hydrochlorothiazide.
- Father: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), end-stage renal disease age 62

He does not smoke and drinks alcohol socially.

The patient with ADPKD and hypertension, followed in nephrology and internal medicine, presents with progressive shortness of breath and reduced exercise tolerance over the past few months and pounding sensations in his chest, especially when lying on his left side.
He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and has not seen a physician in several years.
- Father: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), end-stage renal disease age 62
- Paternal grandfather: Cerebral aneurysm rupture, death age 58
The carotid upstroke is brisk, and there is visible pulsation of the nail beds with gentle compression.
Echocardiography reveals aneurysm of the ascending aorta.
Chest x-ray shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette but clear lung fields.
The patient is referred for further cardiologic assessment.

The patient is a 48-year-old male with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension who presents to the emergency department with progression of symptoms previously evaluated in Cardiology six months prior.
He reports recurrent palpitations and complains of shortness of breath and fatigue that has progressively worsened over the past 6 months.
He denies chest pain, syncope, or edema.
His palpitations are described as rapid and regular, occurring several times a week and sometimes lasting for hours.
His past medical history is significant for hypertension, which is currently untreated.
- Father: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), end-stage renal disease age 62
- Paternal grandfather: Cerebral aneurysm rupture, death age 58
On physical examination, his blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg, heart rate is 130 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
His jugular venous pressure is not elevated, and lung auscultation reveals no crackles.
Cardiac examination reveals a regular tachycardia without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
An echocardiogram demonstrates a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 35%.
An ECG shows atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction.

lines: Progressive fatigue and a painless mass in his left neck

This 49-year-old male with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and hypertension, previously evaluated for fatigue and tachycardia, presents with a 2-month history of progressive fatigue and a painless mass in his left neck.
His past medical history is significant for hypertension, controlled with lisinopril.
- Father: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), end-stage renal disease age 62
- Paternal grandfather: Cerebral aneurysm rupture, death age 58
He denies fever, night sweats, or weight loss.
On physical examination, a 3 cm firm, non-tender lymph node is palpable in the left supraclavicular area.
The remainder of the examination is unremarkable.
- Complete blood count (CBC): within normal limits
Chest X-ray: No mediastinal widening or lung lesions
The PET scan has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80% for detecting NHL involvement.
The prevalence of distant disease in patients with newly diagnosed NHL at this stage is 30%.
The PET scan results come back positive for distant disease.
An excisional biopsy of the lymph node is performed, and the pathology report indicates non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL).
The oncologist recommends a positron emission tomography (PET) scan to evaluate for distant disease.
